title: Rock Tech secures fixed buyer for Canadian lithium - electrive.com
content:
Rock Tech Lithium has signed a binding offtake agreement with Geneva-based commodity trader Transamine for its Georgia Lake project in Ontario. The partnership secures the commercial marketing of the lithium mined there and includes prepayment financing of up to $80 million USD.
Analysis of spodumene from the Georgia Lake project under the UV laser
Image: Stark Resources
The agreement covers the entire planned production of the Georgia Lake project in Ontario. From 2028, Rock Tech Lithium will supply Transamine with up to 100,000 dry metric tonnes of spodumene concentrate annually over an initial seven-year term. This concentrate is a powder produced from spodumene ore mined on-site, which contains a high proportion of lithium oxide (typically around 6 per cent). Battery-grade lithium for electric vehicles can be extracted from it in further processing steps.
The agreement includes a variable delivery volume. In the initial months of the contract, 50,000 tonnes are planned, before the volume increases to the annual maximum of 100,000 tonnes during regular operations. Pricing is based on internationally recognised market benchmarks for spodumene concentrate. The parties have also agreed on an option to extend the contract by up to five additional years.
A key element of the contract is the option for further processing. Rock Tech reserves the right to refine the spodumene concentrate into battery-grade chemicals at its
planned lithium converter in Red Rock
(near the Canadian mine). In such a case, the agreement would convert into a take-or-pay contract for lithium hydroxide or lithium carbonate with Transamine.
To support project development, Transamine is providing an upfront payment facility of up to $80 million USD. Disbursement is subject to strict conditions, including securing full equity financing for the project and obtaining all environmental and operational permits.
CEO Mirco Wojnarowicz describes the contract as a strategic milestone: “This agreement demonstrates how Rock Tech is turning critical minerals ambition into execution. It provides a long-term, commercial foundation for the Georgia Lake mine’s future production, strengthens our financing pathway, and – together with the prepayment facility – brings us another step closer to building the integrated mine-to-converter platform with the flexibility to convert raw material into battery-grade lithium chemicals through our Red Rock Lithium Converter.”
Repayment of the upfront payment will be made over a 24-month period from the first commercial delivery through direct offsetting against the concentrate volumes. Any remaining balances after this period must be settled in cash.
Rock Tech Lithium is active not only in Canada but also in Germany. In Germany, the company does not plan to mine lithium itself but instead aims to build a lithium converter in Guben, Brandenburg. However, the major hurdle for constructing the planned facility lies in the expected investment costs of €750 million euros – and as we saw recently, the young company
cannot shoulder this on its own
. Production was originally scheduled to start in 2027, but realistically, 2029 is now the earliest feasible date. The targeted production volume is expected to suffice for around 30GWh of battery capacity or approximately 500,000 EVs per year.

title: Gotion eyes stake in PowerCo’s Spanish battery cell factory - electrive.com
content:
VW subsidiary PowerCo's battery cell factory in Spain could soon become a joint venture with Gotion before construction is even complete. According to a Spanish media report, VW is considering bringing its Chinese stakeholder on board at the site near Valencia.
This is what PowerCo's cell factory in Sagunt is expected to look like
Image: Volkswagen
As reported by the Spanish trade publication
La Tribuna de Automoción
, the Volkswagen Group is currently in advanced negotiations with its partner Gotion regarding the acquisition of a majority stake in the battery cell factory under construction in Sagunto, which – being near Valencia – PowerCo refers to as Gigafactory Valencia. According to sources, discussions have advanced well, and the Chinese group’s CEO, Zhen Li, has reportedly made high-level visits to the site.
At the heart of negotiations – which are being led by VW’s Board Member for Technology, Thomas Schmall – is the establishment of a joint venture. Under this arrangement, Gotion would take control of the Valencia plant, while PowerCo would remain as a minority shareholder. For Volkswagen, the factory is strategically indispensable, as it is to supply the company’s Spanish and Portuguese vehicle plants with the
Unified Cell
for EVs – which is already in production in Salzgitter.
A potential partnership between VW, PowerCo, and Gotion is not new to the industry. Volkswagen is the largest shareholder in the Chinese company, holding around a quarter of its shares, and Gotion ranks among the global top five battery cell manufacturers. However, as the battery cell factory in Sagunto is not yet operational, Gotion currently supplies cells for models produced in Spain, such as the
, from its factory in Hefei, China. Series production of the Unified Cell
began there in November 2025
. Previously, Gotion had served as a technology partner for the development of the Unified Cell and the construction of PowerCo’s cell production facility in Salzgitter, which reportedly involved hundreds of Chinese specialists.
If Gotion’s entry into the project succeeds, it could expand the customer base of the Valencia factory. According to industry sources, Gotion aims to supply other automotive manufacturers in Spain in the future, with Ford’s plant in Almussafes mentioned as a potential customer. This comes as the Chinese carmaker Geely is currently
planning to take a stake
in the plant.
Meanwhile, the Sagunto project is facing delays. According to sources, the start of pre-series production has been pushed back to December 2026, while series production was not expected to begin before summer 2027. Additionally, staff recruitment is behind schedule: currently, only 50 of the 500 employees required for pre-series production have been hired. PowerCo España declined to comment on market speculation but emphasised to
La Tribuna de Automoción
its unwavering commitment to the site and its swift implementation.
In response to an inquiry from
Automobilwoche
, PowerCo stated that it “regularly reviews strategic opportunities, including potential collaborations with partners.” A spokesperson added: “However, we have no plans to relinquish control of Gigafactory Valencia. PowerCo is fully committed to the Gigafactory in Sagunto and will continue to drive its development at pace.” This statement does not rule out Gotion’s involvement in the project but suggests that PowerCo would retain a majority stake in such a scenario.
Regardless of developments in Sagunto, Gotion is also advancing its plans for a
factory in Valladolid, Spain
. Following recent funding approvals under the Perte-VEC programme, a facility for cathodes and battery recycling is set to be established first.

title: BMW to launch series production of iX5 batteries in December - electrive.com
content:
The BMW Group is preparing to launch series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) batteries for electric vehicles – starting with high-voltage batteries for the
all-electric BMW iX5
, which will begin at its Woodruff plant this December. The facility is a cornerstone for the North American market and was built near the Spartanburg vehicle plant, where the iX5 will be manufactured, in line with the ‘Local for Local’ principle. From there, the vehicle will also be exported to Europe.
To achieve this, the carmaker has implemented cutting-edge processes. The new cylindrical cells in the 46120 format
are integrated directly into the battery pack using the ‘Cell-to-Pack’ method. All production steps are monitored seamlessly in real time. Specially developed AI assistants process data alongside more than 300 employees and 250 robots to ensure zero-defect production.
Even during the planning and ramp-up phases, BMW consistently relied on digital tools. Digital twins and virtual reality applications facilitated factory planning, while employees completed a specially developed VR training programme. This allowed them to practice real-world processes and equipment operations in a highly detailed virtual environment.
“Plant Woodruff plays a key role in the ramp-up of electromobility in the US,” said BMW Production Director Raymond Wittmann. “With our Gen6 high-voltage battery, we’re not only taking a major technological leap – we are also setting new standards in production. In Woodruff, we are combining cutting-edge processes, artificial intelligence and the expertise of our employees to create a production facility designed for the highest quality.”
These AESC cylindrical cells in the 46120 format are integrated into BMW battery systems
Technologically, the system is based on an 800-volt architecture. The BMW iX5 60 xDrive offers a usable net energy content of 144kWh in the USA and 141kWh in Europe. In terms of sustainability, the Gen6 battery cell reduces CO₂e emissions by around 28 per cent compared to the previous generation. This reduction is achieved through the use of secondary materials for cobalt, lithium, and nickel, as well as green electricity in cell production. The Woodruff plant itself operates entirely without fossil fuels during normal operations, while its material handling equipment is powered by hydrogen.
The foundation for the project was laid in June 2023 with the
groundbreaking ceremony for the Woodruff plant
. Construction commenced in September 2023, followed by the installation of equipment in autumn 2024. Pre-series test runs began in summer 2025. The investments in Woodruff are part of a comprehensive US strategy, in which BMW invested approximately $1.7 billion in electromobility in the Spartanburg region, including partnerships with local cell suppliers such as AESC.

title: EnerSys to produce ‘defence‑focused Li cells’ in revised gigafactory plans – Batteries International
content: EnerSys has refocused plans for its $500 million battery cell gigafactory in South Carolina for US defence needs — and is ending a tech partnership with French Li cells developer Verkor. The US lead and lithium major has also revised the plant’s construction schedule to now start work in the first half of fiscal 2028, instead of early 2025 as announced when South Carolina was selected to host the 4GWh per annum facility in 2024. The battery maker’s revised plans were confirmed on July 23. EnerSys also said it now expects to receive a revised grant of $150 million from the Department of Energy. Full production is now set to start around three years after construction begins. Under the updated plans, EnerSys expects the 500,000ft 2 facility to have an initial production capacity of around 1GWh, using federal, state, local funding and operating cash flow to fund the facility’s capital cost. The plant will support US defence requirements for secure, foreign entity of concern compliant lithium ion cells and strengthen the country’s supply chain. Given the facility’s refined defence-focused scope, EnerSys said it intends to “transition away from its technology relationship with Verkor” and does not expect the French company to serve as the project’s technology partner. Instead, EnerSys will draw on support from what it described as its decades-long, established technology partnerships within its existing aerospace and defence supply base. President and CEO Shawn O’Connell said the revised strategy builds on the firm’s role as a trusted supplier of stored energy solutions for US defence applications. “By dedicating this facility to defence‑focused lithium cell development and manufacturing, we will further strengthen a secure, resilient, domestically sourced supply chain aligned with evolving US national security requirements.” The post EnerSys to produce ‘defence‑focused Li cells’ in revised gigafactory plans appeared first on Batteries International .

title: Germany’s Varta files for insolvency in restructuring bid   – Batteries International
content: German battery maker Varta has filed applications for insolvency as part of plans for the long-term restructuring of the troubled company. Varta said it filed the self-administration applications in Stuttgart on July 23 and told employees the following day — citing “significantly deteriorated market conditions, weaker demand and negative exchange rate effects”. A recent decision by a key customer to end cooperation was also a contributing factor, Varta said. In addition to the parent company (Varta AG) the operating units Varta Microbattery in Ellwangen, Varta Micro Production in Nördlingen and Varta Storage are affected. Preliminary insolvency proceedings in self-administration have also been launched for Varta Microbattery. The Varta Consumer Batteries business unit and its associated companies, which are legally and operationally separate and financially independent, are expressly excluded from the applications. Varta said its existing group structures and complex internal inter-dependencies had made it difficult to effectively implement necessary restructuring measures and require additional liquidity. This led to a “structural financing gap” at the level of the parent company, against a background of an ongoing restructuring review, especially with regard to the further development of the company from 2027. The Stuttgart District Court has appointed Tobias Wahl, of the German law firm Anchor, as provisional administrator — with the aim of securing the economic future of the company and the sustainable continuation of business operations. Varta CEO Michael Ostermann said the court move was an unavoidable step despite earlier restructuring efforts. “Varta has had to contend with major challenges in recent quarters. We on the board of management and the executive board are aware of the overall responsibility for employees, customers, suppliers and financiers and are working with all our might to preserve as many jobs as possible, to enable sustainable continuation and to create the best possible prospects for all stakeholders.” Ostermann said the market for energy storage systems continues to be an industry of the future that needs strong domestic suppliers and technology leaders such as Varta. The insolvency move comes just over a year after Varta unveiled a multi-million-euro liquidity boost in the latest steps of a restructuring plan to “guarantee” battery tech production and research in Europe. Earlier this year, Ostermann discussed his plans for Varta’s future with Batteries International editor Shona Sibary. He said then it had been a “challenging year”, adding: “As you can imagine, we’ve been having seven-day-a-week negotiations with lenders. The very first priority for me was to get the financial situation stabilised. “We have become a little bit too fat in recent years. We had way too many overheads, and we are now doing some operational restructuring by making the organisation and our processes slimmer to be able to make faster decisions, because this has sometimes been too slow.” Read that exclusive interview here . title: China’s Gotion secures €100m African bank loan for Morocco gigafactory – Batteries International
content:
News, Other Chemistries
China’s Gotion secures €100m African bank loan for Morocco gigafactory
–  July 27, 2026 06:27 pm BST
The African Development Bank Group has given the green light for a €100 million ($114 million) loan to the North African subsidiary of China’s Gotion Power for its LFP battery gigafactory project in Morocco.
The bank confirmed the loan agreement with Gotion Power Morocco on July 24 — and said it also planned to crowd in an extra €141 million from financial partners to support the eventual 100GWh capacity project in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra Free Trade Zone.
Gotion started initial infrastructure work at the site in May 2025, saying the gigafactory would be the first such plant in the Middle East and North African region, capable of producing 10GWh of battery cells and packs for EVs on completion of its first phase.
Total investment in the first phase of the plant is projected at around €1.3 billion.
Bank group VP for power, energy, climate and green growth, Kevin Kariuki, said: “Battery storage is the missing link in Africa’s clean energy transition. A facility of this scale, powered primarily by renewable energy, strengthens the foundations for the large-scale integration of solar and wind power, which our grids increasingly depend on.”
Achraf Tarsim, the bank group’s country manager for Morocco, said the gigafactory would help foster an African industrial ecosystem for batteries and EVs while promoting domestic processing of minerals critical to the energy transition.
The loan deal comes less than two years after Gotion announced a
with Saudi energy giant Acwa Power — which will develop a 500MW wind facility and 2,000MWh BESS to support the gigafactory.
Earlier this month, the head of the African Export-Import Bank
the continent’s leaders to choke off supplies of battery raw materials such as lithium to other countries and instead power homegrown African EV battery industries.
Afreximbank president and board chairman George Elombi said Africa’s economic sovereignty could only be achieved by industrialising at scale — processing its own resources and securing financing to develop batteries “on its own terms”.

title: Qnetic announces Pulsar prototype flywheel tech milestones – Batteries International
content:
Energy Storage, News
Qnetic announces Pulsar prototype flywheel tech milestones
–  July 27, 2026 06:26 pm BST
Qnetic's 200-kWh Pulsar system
US-headquartered flywheel tech developer Qnetic has begun assembly of its first full-scale 200kWh ‘Pulsar’ prototype and has started building a test facility in China.
Qnetic said on July 16 its test technology centre in Shanghai represents a million-dollar-plus investment that will serve as the company’s primary site for validating the performance, safety, and reliability of its next-generation flywheel systems.
Significant excavation and foundation work is taking place, with installation of the Pulsar prototype planned on completion of the facility, followed by technical validation.
The milestones are major steps toward commercial deployment of Qnetic’s technology — which the company claims is designed to provide long-duration energy storage without the degradation, fire risk or dependence on critical minerals associated with conventional lithium ion batteries.
Pulsar is being developed for applications including data centres, renewable energy time-shifting, grid balancing, microgrids, and industrial power resilience.
Qnetic is working with an undisclosed partner specialised in spin-test technologies to deliver a system the firm said will offer grid and commercial operators a durable, lower-lifetime-cost alternative for multi-hour energy storage.
Qnetic’s flywheel systems can complement or replace lithium ion batteries in applications where long asset life, unlimited cycling, sustainability and predictable lifetime economics are critical, the company said.
Pulsar operates at extreme speeds and in vacuum conditions, “pushing conventional motor design to its limits”.
CEO Michael Pratt said: “Building the world’s largest flywheel test cell while bringing our first Pulsar system into validation demonstrates both the maturity of our technology and our confidence in its commercial potential.”
Qnetic announced in March 2026 it had raised $7.1 million over the past year to accelerate commercialisation, including $5 million to launch manufacturing in the US and deploy its first flywheel energy storage systems.

title: Innovation over imitation: how to win the global battery race with China – Batteries International
content: China did not invent the Li-ion battery, nor was it first to commercialise the technology, but it was quick to understand that dominating supply was of strategic importance and took less than 20 years to get there. For the West to compete the focus must be on discovering breakthrough chemistries and accelerating the progression from lab to volume production . Like any commodity market, the global lithium-ion battery sector is defined by massive numbers and a scale that is truly astonishing: in 2025 the market was worth more than $150 billion and the total output was 1,600GWh of capacity. But sourcing is decidedly one-sided. More than 80% of batteries that year were manufactured in China. Of those made elsewhere, the majority relied on materials supplied by China. This dependency has long been recognised but most attempts to compete have so far ended in failure. So how can the rest of the world catch-up? Not through scale alone, and certainly not by trying to replicate what China has already achieved. As an industry we must focus on innovation because where we can lead is by developing next-generation chemistries, not ramping-up production of the last ones. Bloomberg reports that European and North American battery packs cost 56% and 44% more respectively than those from China, and expects the next wave of cost reduction to come from new cathode materials and cell designs. Accelerated development Wildcat’s High Throughput Platform (HTP) is a key enabler for this. (Wildcat Discovery Technologies was acquired by Holyvolt earlier this year.) Based on techniques first developed in the pharmaceutical industry to accelerate synthesis, testing, and commercialisation of new drugs, Wildcat was first to apply them to battery chemistry discovery more than 18 years ago and has optimised the method ever since. Where existing R&D processes can evaluate several potential new chemistries in a year, Wildcat’s can screen several thousands in a week. The value of this unrivalled speed is compounded by the data it creates because the results of every single experiment performed to date have been recorded. These two assets when integrated with AI will deliver a data-led step-change in capability by creating an intelligent discovery engine that can find the next breakthrough first, accurately predict they key performance attributes, then validate them. The value of this is far greater than just enabling better batteries. With materials accounting for more than 82% of cell production costs, focusing development efforts here will have a strong influence on competitiveness with China — and moving away from critical minerals such as cobalt and nickel. Built-in advantages In parallel, Holyvolt’s screen-printing process and high solid content, water-based technology for electrode manufacturing offers a cost-effective, sustainable, and scalable route to production that does not suffer the same investment risks as conventional gigafactories. Designed for lower CAPEX spend than the dominant slot-die process, screen printing at gigawatt scale cuts electrode coating costs by at least half for a given line speed and production capacity. Further CAPEX savings come from smaller drying ovens — those used for NMP solvent-based slurries are as long as a football pitch — and smaller dry rooms. This in turn enables factory footprint to be smaller, and with every square metre costing several thousand dollarsb, any reduction in size is worthwhile. Downsizing plants and equipment also reduces OPEX. Drying ovens for existing wet coating processes draw megawatts of power and need complex solvent recovery systems to capture and purify toxic and highly flammable NMP vapours. This stage of manufacturing and the dry room are the most energy-intensive of all, accounting for more than 75% of the total. Screen printing eliminates NMP altogether, making it an inherently cleaner technology, and we believe we can reduce that energy consumption by half. This combination of next-generation cell chemistries, cutting-edge manufacturing techniques, and streamlined plants provides Western cell companies a viable, cost-efficient, scalable route into high volume production without the inherent risk of the current gigafactory model. These qualities are also becoming increasingly attractive due to burgeoning regulatory requirements for sustainability, and growing demand from governments and industry for sovereign capability. The ability to compress timescales from discovery to pilot production and robust, efficient, cost-effective scale-up is fundamental to removing the bottleneck that acts as a brake on the pace of innovation in Europe and the US. The technical solutions exist, and collaborative development will enable successful industrialisation. To win we must stop looking back at what China has achieved and redouble our efforts to find the chemistries we need for the future. Otherwise, we will still be playing catch-up rather than taking the lead in a race we cannot afford to lose. title: How Battery Validation is Shaping the Future Grid
content:
Viridi and ORNL collaborate to test and validate advanced battery systems, enhancing grid resilience, safety, and modernization efforts.
July 28, 2026
Viridi's RPS 150 battery energy storage system installed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory's (ORNL) Power Distribution Field Test Site.
Viridi, a company specializing in
battery energy storage systems
(BESS), has partnered with Oak Ridge National Laboratory (
), a DOE national laboratory, to support research into next-generation utility grid technologies. This collaboration is part of a broader effort to enhance grid resilience and reliability, addressing the growing challenges of modernizing the US electric grid. The partnership highlights the importance of real-world testing, safety innovation, and industry validation in advancing energy storage solutions.
This collaboration involves integrating
’s RPS 150 battery energy storage system into ORNL’s Grid Research Innovation and Development Center (
). The system was selected as part of a DOE project focused on resource integration and evaluation. This initiative is designed to address the complexities of aging grid infrastructure, the integration of distributed energy resources (DERs) such as solar panels, wind turbines, and small-scale energy storage systems, and the need to improve resilience against disruptions. Testing for the project has now concluded, and ORNL is expected to present the findings in the coming months.
Startups Pitch Investors to Transform the Battery Industry
One of the most critical aspects of this partnership is the opportunity to validate battery technology under real-world conditions. Real-world validation is a critical step in building confidence among utilities and investors to adopt advanced energy storage solutions. While initial testing of ORNL’s grid control systems was conducted in a controlled laboratory environment using emulated energy sources, real-world testing provides a better understanding of complex equipment interactions and real-world battery charging dynamics.
’s RPS 150 battery system was installed at GRID-C’s Power Distribution Field Test Site to support this phase of the research. The system was integrated with ORNL’s converter technology to evaluate its performance under real-world conditions. This step was essential for identifying and addressing issues that arise from complex equipment interactions and the dynamic nature of battery charging and discharging.
“This project bridges an important gap by integrating real electrical equipment to understand realistic performance challenges, proving the robustness of ORNL’s new control strategies and AC/DC architecture for supporting the future grid,” stated Dr. Madhu Sudhan Chinthavali, Electrical Systems Integration Program Manager at ORNL.
Safety remains a top priority in the deployment of battery energy storage systems, and this collaboration underscores the importance of addressing safety challenges. Advanced technologies, such as those designed to prevent thermal runaway and reduce the risk of battery fires, are essential for ensuring the safe integration of energy storage systems into critical infrastructure.
Breaking Down the Limits of Solid-State Battery Performance
The successful integration of the battery system with ORNL’s grid control systems highlights the importance of robust safety measures in energy storage technology. As energy storage systems become more widespread, ensuring their safety and reliability will remain a key focus for the industry.
Industry validation plays a crucial role in advancing energy storage technologies and grid modernization efforts. Collaborations with national laboratories, such as ORNL, provide an opportunity to test emerging technologies under rigorous conditions, ensuring they meet the highest standards for performance, safety, and reliability. The findings from such projects offer valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities associated with grid modernization. Partnerships between private companies and research institutions are essential for driving progress and ensuring that new technologies are ready to meet the demands of a rapidly evolving energy landscape.

title: EcoVadis & Schneider: Decarbonising Pharma Supply Chains
content:
EcoVadis & Schneider: Decarbonising Pharma Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
EcoVadis links its Responsible Health Initiative with Schneider Electric's Energize programme to boost supplier climate action in pharma supply chains
EcoVadis has confirmed a new collaboration between its Responsible Health Initiative (RHI) and the Energize programme.
Energize is designed and delivered by SE Advisory Services, which is Schneider Electric's global consulting practice.
The collaboration is intended to support
decarbonisation across pharmaceutical supply chains
. Suppliers linked to the RHI can now access training and guidance for climate action through Energize.
According to EcoVadis, Scope 3 emissions are 21 times larger than Scope 1 and Scope 2 combined for the average company.
The organisation states that ignoring these emissions could cost companies more than US$500bn in annual liabilities by 2030.
Within the healthcare sector specifically, EcoVadis reports that only 6% of companies have a plan in place to move toward
low-carbon operations and supply chains
This gap could mean there is scope for healthcare companies to develop emissions reduction plans and engage further with climate action.
Steve Wilhite, Executive Vice President at SE Advisory Services, writes on LinkedIn: "Supply chain decarbonisation is too complex for any one organisation to tackle alone. So we're celebrating a new milestone in our collaboration with EcoVadis.
"Suppliers participating in their Responsible Health Initiative can now join our Energize programme. Led by SE Advisory Services, the programme provides training for decarbonisation efforts across global pharmaceutical value chains.
"Bringing together healthcare leaders, suppliers and sustainability experts creates a powerful opportunity to address some of the most significant Scope 3 emissions challenges facing the industry. Collaboration remains one of the most effective ways to scale climate action."
The Responsible Health Initiative was founded in 2018 by a group of healthcare, biotech and pharmaceutical companies with the aim of advancing sustainability across their value chains.
The initiative allows industry leaders to share best practices and processes. This could foster common understanding between companies looking to improve sustainability performance.
Members aim to strengthen supplier outreach and expand visibility of the wider health sector's supply chain sustainability performance. The setup allows companies to engage directly with industry peers and external stakeholders.
Through the new collaboration, suppliers can build plans to transition toward renewable energy. The RHI also offers training and personalised guidance intended to help suppliers build confidence with carbon management and sustainability reporting.
Fernanda Campos Helmeister, Supply Chain Decarbonisation Programme Manager at SE Advisory Services, says: "The Responsible Health Initiative's new collaboration with SE Advisory Services's Energize programme makes renewable energy adoption much more accessible across geographies, supporting decarbonisation efforts across the pharma and healthcare value chain as a whole."
brings together 27 global pharmaceutical companies with the goal of engaging hundreds of suppliers in climate action.
The programme is focused on the decarbonisation of the pharmaceutical value chain.
Through the link with the RHI, suppliers can now join Energize to access education, digital tools and advisory services delivered by teams at Schneider Electric.
Sponsor companies involved in Energize include AstraZeneca, GSK, Haleon, Sanofi, Novo Nordisk, Johnson & Johnson and Novartis among others.
"As we confront the urgent reality of the climate crisis, we understand that collective action is essential," says Katiana Iavarone, Chief Procurement Officer at UCB, one of the sponsor companies.
"At UCB, we're committed to driving the ecological transition also through renewable energy. By forging key partnerships, such as the Energize programme, we strive to achieve significant decarbonisation outcomes and extend our impact beyond what we can achieve alone.
"Together, we're building a more sustainable future."

title: Orchestrating Supply Chains with Siemens & NVIDIA AI
content:
Orchestrating Supply Chains with Siemens & NVIDIA AI
Prioritise Us
Siemens and NVIDIA expand their collaboration to advance self-verifying agentic AI workflows ahead of Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit in September
With global supply chain leaders facing complexity and volatility at never before seen levels,
manual processes and fragmented digital designs
are becoming increasingly useless. To stay ahead of competitors, organisations are looking to speed up their transition towards end-to-end supply chain orchestration.
Orchestration enables companies to predict disruptions and respond automatically in real time, and leading technology innovators are bringing this concept into the hardware and engineering foundation of modern supply chains.
Siemens has announced its strategic collaboration with NVIDIA to introduce self-verifying agentic AI workflows. With this technology, it aims to streamline high-tech
manufacturing pipelines
and optimise component production.
Key Facts: What you need to know about the Siemens & NVIDIA partnership
Agentic AI integration: Siemens EDA and NVIDIA expanded their partnership at DAC 2026 to bring self-verifying agentic AI to semiconductor and PCB design.
Full-stack performance: Combining Siemens Fuse EDA with NVIDIA NeMo Gym, Nemotron models and CUDA-X accelerates library characterisation by more than 10x.
Self-verifying execution: Autonomous AI agents execute multi-step engineering tasks while validating outcomes against physics-based verification engines.
Enterprise security: Built on NVIDIA OpenShell to deliver sandboxed, secure execution with strict access controls and full auditability for hardware IP.
This new development comes as industry leaders prepare to gather at Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit in September 2026 where they will discuss how advanced automation and orchestration
are reshaping the way we operate on a global scale.
secure your ticket now
to be part of this important conversation.
As part of the new collaboration between Siemens and NVIDIA, Siemens’s Fuse EDA AI Agent system will be paired with NVIDIA’s AI infrastructure to reshape semiconductor and printed circuit board (PCB) design workflows.

title: DP World: Developing Flexibility Across Global Trade Routes
content:
DP World: Developing Flexibility Across Global Trade Routes
Prioritise Us
DP World is expanding the UAE gateway network, with two new terminals at the Fujairah Ports Authority, working to drive greater connectivity in trade
is working to provide greater connectivity and flexibility to customers in UAE, through the expansion of the Fujairah Ports Authority.
Amid ongoing geopolitical volatility and disruption in the critical trade route of the
Strait of Hormuz
, logistics companies around the world are looking to better support their customers.
This new development will support UAE capacity growth and will help streamline global trade.
The Al Rugaylat and Dibba terminals will bring world-class operating capability, expanded capacity and new investment to the emirate.
H.H. Sheikh Saleh Bin Mohamed Al Sharqi, Chairman, Fujairah Ports Authority
The Port of Fujairah is the only multi-purpose seaport on the eastern coastline of UAE, located 70 nautical miles from the Strait of Hormuz. Due to this,it has been strategically located in order to provide essential access to trade. The port acts as an economic link between Europe and Asia, as well as providing more trade opportunities to India and North East Africa.
To increase operation capacity,
has developed an agreement with the Fujairah Ports Authority, to develop two new terminals, as part of a 50-year deal. The Al Rugaylat terminal is a multi-purpose and container terminal, and DP World will also operate the Dibba General Cargo terminal. DP World currently operates four ports and facilities in the UAE; Jebel Ali, Mina Al Hamriya, Mina Rashid and Dubai Creek & Deira Wharfage.
"Locating the new terminal outside the Straight of Hormuz would enable ships to sail in relative safety; the construction of the port was effectively a response to the closure of the Straight in the 1980s Iran-Iraq ware. However, the 12 May 2019 attack as well as more recent issues shows that it is not immune from danger," explains Emile Naus, Partner at BearingPoint in a statement to Supply Chain Digital.
The new terminals will create a deep-water trade gateway on the east coast of UAE, with capabilities of handling Ultra Large Container Vessels. Al Rugaylat will be able to handle up to 2.5 million TEUs every year, as well as 1.7 million tonnes of general cargo and 190,000 Car Equivalent Units (CEUs). Dibba will manage up to 3.6 million tonnes of annual general cargo capacity.
"The partnership with DP World marks an important milestone in Fujairah's continued development as one of the region's most important maritime gateways," says H.H. Sheikh Saleh Bin Mohamed Al Sharqi, Chairman, Fujairah Ports Authority.
"The Al Rugaylat and Dibba terminals will bring world-class operating capability, expanded capacity and new investment to the emirate. We look forward to working with DP World to deliver a project that will benefit customers, communities and the UAE's wider economy."
Construction is expected to take 24 to 30 months
Capacity for DP World in the UAE will reach 22 million TEUs
Al Rugaylat will handle 1.7 million tonnes of general cargo and 190,000 CEUs every year
Dibba will increase general cargo capacity by 3.6 million tonnes annually
The Port of Jebel Ali and the Port of Fujairah are 152 km apart by road
There are approximately 245 nautical miles between Jebel Ali Port and the Port of Fujairah
It is anticipated that the new logistics zone will drive further investment, employment and long-term economic opportunity to the region. Moreover, it will expand DP World's capabilities of supporting global trade.
Within the UAE, DP World currently has a total container handling capacity of 19.4 million TEUs, but with this expansion, it will reach almost 22 million TEUs. It will be able to deliver as a global integrated platform across global supply chains, with more capacity amid
growing demand
for trade. With the rise of ecommerce and a growing need of supply chain diversification, ports and terminals around the world are challenged with growing their operational capacity.
It offers greater choice of destination for cargo owners, as well as more flexibility when operating in periods of high demand, as well as more supply chain resilience amid global volatility.
"The UAE has been at the heart of DP World's story for more than four decades, and this investment reflects our confidence in its future as one of the world's leading trade and logistics hubs," explains H.E. Essa Kazim, Chairman, DP World.
"Building on the
strength of Jebel Ali
, this development deepens our commitment to the UAE and reinforces the country's strategic role in global trade."
As DP World operates as a multimodal logistics company, the Fujairah terminals will be connected to Jebel Ali through its inland logistics network. This allows for a more integrated end-to-end supply chain across the UAE, with
expanded capabilities
of moving cargo efficiently between ports, logistics hubs and end markets.
Emile, however, warns of logistics concerns which could occur within the new terminal, stating, "the port is more exposed than the existing Jebel Ali facilities, with direct exposure to the weather in the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea", and that due to its elevation, there are logistical issues regarding road freight.
However, he also points to the anticipated risk to Jebel Ali that DP World may be facing amid ongoing geopolitical turbulence.
Construction of these ports is anticipated to take 24 to 30 months.

title: Tesla buys 90% of a 509 MW Arizona solar and storage project
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 28 2026 - 8:32 am PT
Tesla has signed a long-term deal to buy 90% of the output of Project Sterling, a big solar and battery plant going up in Arizona.
The project pairs 509 MW of solar with a 360 MW battery, and it’s being built by ContourGlobal, the power producer owned by private equity firm KKR. It’s expected online in 2028.
Neither company disclosed financial terms. ContourGlobal will keep and trade the remaining 10% of the output itself. Deals like this usually run 10 to 15 years, so Tesla is locking in Arizona clean power well into the 2030s. It’s the first agreement between the two companies, and ContourGlobal, which picked up the project in late 2024, calls Project Sterling the largest renewable asset in its portfolio.
The plant connects to the Western Area Power Administration grid, which gives it access to California markets. The 360 MW battery is a four-hour system, roughly 1,440 MWh of storage, enough to keep pushing solar power onto the grid after the sun goes down.
This is the second large solar PPA Tesla signed today. Earlier, Tesla and Spanish developer Zelestra confirmed a deal for
the entire output of a 140 MW solar farm in Texas
. Put the two together, and Tesla contracted more than 640 MW of third-party solar, plus 360 MW of battery storage, in a single day.
The reason is the same one driving every hyperscaler right now. Electricity demand is climbing fast, AI data centers are tightening US power markets, and Tesla has its own growing load to feed, from Gigafactory Texas to its expanding AI compute. It needs cheap, clean power, and it needs it locked in.
Here’s the part that stands out. Tesla builds the Megapack, the best-selling grid battery in the world, and it already has
one of Arizona’s largest Megapack installations
online. It sells solar panels and is
building a 100-GW solar panel factory in Texas
Yet for Project Sterling, Tesla is buying both the solar and the storage from a KKR-owned developer rather than building it. Neither company said whose batteries the plant will use.
That’s the tradeoff of being a power buyer instead of a power builder. Tesla makes the hardware, but it doesn’t develop and operate utility-scale solar-plus-storage plants at the speed it now needs. So it signs PPAs, the same as Meta and Google.
Two solar PPAs in one day tells you how seriously Tesla is taking its own power problem. Its electricity needs are growing (factories, and now AI compute that eats megawatts), and it can’t wait. Locking in more than 640 MW of solar and a big battery for the late 2020s is a smart, unglamorous move.
But the irony from this morning’s Texas deal is even sharper here. Tesla doesn’t just sell solar panels. It makes some of the best grid battery on the market, and it’s buying a 360 MW battery’s worth of stored solar from someone else – though I. wouldn’t be surprised if the projects ends up using Megapacks, which would mean Tesla would be buying back battery capacity that it manufactured.
There’s a version of Tesla that builds Project Sterling itself, with its own panels and its own Megapacks, and books the whole thing as a win for its energy business. That’s not the Tesla we have. It gutted its solar arm years ago and is only now rebuilding.

content:

The Racco went on sale as the “world’s first SDV-based” light EV,
said, with a low starting price of around $13,000.
BYD held a launch event for the Racco on Tuesday, its first electric kei car aimed at Japan’s light vehicle market,
The market has been historically dominated by domestic brands like Honda, Suzuki, and Nissan, but BYD believes it can crack open the market.
Kei cars are the most popular vehicle in Japan because they are affordable, efficient, and easy to maneuver around tight city streets.
BYD’s Racco checks all the boxes. The electric kei car is available in two models: 200 or 300, starting at just ¥2,145,000, or about $13,000. Buyers can choose from three different grades: Base, Plus, or Premium.
The base Racco 200 uses a 22.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery with a WLTC driving range of 210 km (130 miles). The higher-priced 300 Plus and Premium trims gain a larger 35.84 kWh battery, providing up to 320 km (199 miles), which BYD said makes it the first kei EV in Japan to offer over 300 km.
Measuring 3,395 mm in length, 1,475 mm in width, and 1,800 mm in height, the Racco is about the size of the Honda N-Box, Japan’s best-selling vehicle for the fourth consecutive year.
While the N-Box is slightly cheaper, starting at ¥1,739,100 ($10,500), BYD said the kei EV is eligible for a ¥150,000 ($900) government subsidy, bringing the Racco’s starting price to ¥1,995,000 ($12,200). BYD is offering leases for as little as ¥19,300 ($115) per month.
The Racco is the “world’s first SDV-based light electric vehicle,” according to BYD, with a redesigned chassis, body, and drive system.
As an SDV-based vehicle, its in-car software can be updated like a smartphone to introduce new features and more.
The interior is based on BYD’s ocean aesthetics cabin design with a 10.1″ floating center infotainment screen and small instrument display.
BYD’s light vehicle development director, Yang Buyi, said
features an “EV-exclusive” Super Tall x Sliding Door design that’s perfect for families with children, married couples, young couples, and everyone in between.
Can BYD’s first electric kei car compete with domestic automakers?
The Racco is cheaper than the Nissan Sakura, Japan’s current best-selling EV, which starts at ¥2,448,600 ($15,000). It also offers a longer driving range than the Sakura, which offers only up to 180 km (111 miles).

title: Mitsubishi's 'all-new' Eclipse Sportback EV is a rebadged Nissan Leaf
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 28 2026 - 7:30 am PT
Mitsubishi is bringing a fully electric vehicle back to North America for the first time in over a decade, and it’s calling the 2027 Eclipse Sportback EV “all-new.”
It isn’t. The Eclipse Sportback is a rebadged next-generation Nissan Leaf, sourced from Mitsubishi’s Alliance partner and reskinned with new bumpers and lights.
Mitsubishi confirmed the vehicle in a press release, describing it as “the global debut of an all-new fully electric vehicle” that will launch across the US and Canada in late summer or early fall 2026, sold through roughly 300 dealer partners in the US.
The company is upfront about where it comes from, at least. The release says the Eclipse Sportback EV is “sourced from Mitsubishi Motors’ Alliance partner Nissan Motor Co, based on the next-generation Nissan LEAF.” So “all-new” is doing a lot of work here.
Not much under the skin. Mitsubishi gives the Eclipse Sportback its own front and rear fascias, a different lighting signature, sporty alloy wheels, and Triple Diamond badging. That’s the extent of it.
Everything mechanical is Leaf. The specs Mitsubishi has shared — a 75 kWh liquid-cooled battery, a native NACS port for Tesla Superchargers, and 150 kW DC fast charging that takes it from 10% to 80% in about 35 minutes — are identical to the
reborn 2026 Nissan Leaf
we drove last year. Same numbers, same hardware.
This isn’t a surprise. We
reported in March
that Mitsubishi was developing a Leaf-based EV for a summer launch, after prototypes were spotted testing with light camouflage. Now it has a name and a face.
Mitsubishi hasn’t sold a real EV in the US since the tiny i-MiEV was discontinued years ago. Its current green push runs through the Outlander PHEV, a plug-in hybrid. So rather than spend years and billions developing an electric crossover from scratch, it’s borrowing one from Nissan and wearing it. This is exactly the kind of badge-engineering the Renault-Nissan-Mitsubishi Alliance exists to enable.
It’s interesting that the company decided to use the Eclipse name. It used to belong to a sport coupe, then got recycled for the Eclipse Cross crossover. Now it’s stretched onto a rebadged Leaf. The nameplate keeps moving; the substance keeps shrinking.
Mitsubishi hasn’t announced range or pricing yet, which are the two numbers buyers actually care about. On the Leaf, EPA range runs from 303 miles on the base S+ down to 259 miles on the top Platinum+ trim, and Nissan starts it at
. Expect Mitsubishi to land somewhere near that, likely a bit higher for the styling.
There’s nothing wrong with a rebadge. The Leaf is a genuinely good, affordable EV now, and putting it in more showrooms through more brands is good for EV adoption. If you like the way the Eclipse Sportback looks better than the Leaf, buy it.
The bigger issue is what this says about Mitsubishi. A rebadge is a fine stopgap, but it’s not a strategy. Nissan controls the platform, the battery, the software, and the roadmap. Mitsubishi controls the grille. If the Alliance ever reshuffles, Mitsubishi is left with a nameplate and no EV. For now it gets a competitive electric crossover without doing the hard part. The question is whether it ever plans to.

title: Yamaha is preparing to launch another electric scooter, design filings show
content:
| Jul 28 2026 - 6:56 am PT
Yamaha may not have found runaway success with its
previous electric scooters
, but new design filings suggest the company isn’t giving up on battery-powered two-wheelers just yet.
As first spotted in Japanese design registration documents and recently reported by
, Yamaha appears to have a new production-ready electric scooter waiting in the wings. While the styling is fairly conservative, the scooter features several engineering choices that set it apart from the growing crowd of electric commuters.
The scooter looks to fall into the 125cc-equivalent category, with proportions similar to Yamaha’s current RayZR 125. But unlike many electric scooters that integrate the motor directly into the rear swingarm, this model appears to use a centrally mounted electric motor driving the rear wheel via a belt. That layout is more reminiscent of typical moto-design and could potentially offer improved weight distribution and suspension performance.
The battery pack also appears to be housed beneath the seat, where it is likely designed to be removable, following the approach Yamaha already uses on its NEO’s electric scooter with swappable batteries. However, Yamaha has used
multiple sizes and styles of removable batteries
in its electric scooters, so it is not clear exactly which model would be employed here.
Another interesting departure from convention is the rear suspension. Rather than mounting the twin shocks near the rear axle as most scooters do, Yamaha has positioned them much farther forward and wider apart, seemingly to accommodate the battery compartment underneath the seat.
Other visible features include a compact TFT display, multiple storage compartments integrated into the front leg shield, and what appears to be a keyless ignition system. The front end also receives a more distinctive lighting signature with four separate headlamps surrounding a central running light.
With the design looking essentially production-ready, the scooter could make its official debut before long. The bigger question, however, is which markets Yamaha would target, and whether those markets have matured enough for Yamaha to find greater success with electric scooters than it did
in previous attempts.

title: Tesla buys the entire output of a new 140 MW Texas solar farm
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 28 2026 - 6:53 am PT
Tesla has signed a long-term power purchase agreement to buy the entire output of a 140-MWac solar farm being built in northeast Texas.
The plant, called Lumen Farm, is being developed by Zelestra, an EQT-backed renewable developer. Construction is expected to start in 2027, with the farm going online in 2029.
Neither company disclosed pricing or what the electricity will power. Zelestra confirmed only that Tesla is taking “the entire output” of the plant. In practice, a 140-MW solar farm in Texas is the kind of clean-power supply a company uses to match a big, growing electricity load — and Tesla has plenty of those in the state, from Gigafactory Texas to its rapidly expanding AI compute.
It’s the second deal between the two companies. In 2024, Zelestra signed a 57-MWac PPA with Tesla covering three solar plants in Spain’s Castilla-La Mancha region. This is their first in the US.
“As a trusted global partner, we can deliver bespoke solutions for clients in multiple geographies,” said Zelestra US CEO Phil North. “As such, we are excited to expand our relationship with Tesla to the US.”
Zelestra isn’t a household name, but it’s become one of the busiest solar developers in Texas. The company runs a portfolio of more than 16 GW of renewable projects and was recently ranked by BloombergNEF among the top 10 corporate clean energy sellers in the world.
Its other big Texas customer is Meta. Over the past year, Zelestra has signed a string of solar PPAs with Meta to feed data centers, including the 180-MWdc Palmera project and the 176-MWdc Skull Creek plant. It also locked in $600 million in green financing for a 440-MW Texas portfolio backed by those Meta contracts.
So Tesla is now buying from the same developer that’s powering Meta’s data centers, in the same grid (ERCOT), for the same reason: a fast-growing electricity load that needs cheap, clean supply. The competition for solar power in Texas is heating up, and Tesla is now on the buyer side of it.
What makes this deal odd is that Tesla is a solar company. It bought SolarCity in 2016, the largest residential solar installer in the US at the time. It sells solar panels and the Solar Roof. It makes the Powerwall and the Megapack, the best-selling grid battery on the market. And it’s now
building a 100-GW solar panel factory near Houston
, in the same state where this Zelestra farm will go up.
And yet, to green its own Texas operations, Tesla is buying power from someone else’s solar farm.
That’s the legacy of Tesla spending years gutting the solar business it paid $2.6 billion for. After the SolarCity deal, deployments collapsed, falling from SolarCity’s peak of roughly 870 MW a year to a fraction of that, as Tesla shut down sales channels and let the business wither. For years, solar was an afterthought while the company poured everything into vehicles and Megapack.
Only recently has Tesla started rebuilding. It
brought back solar leasing
in late 2025,
launched a US-made solar panel
in January, and is now standing up that giant Houston factory. But rebuilding takes time, and Tesla clearly can’t wait for its own utility-scale supply. So it’s buying.

title: Tesla sues Cybertruck supplier amid standoff keeping production hostage
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 28 2026 - 6:00 am PT
Tesla is asking a federal judge for emergency access to a supplier’s plant in Troy, Texas, so it can haul out the tooling it needs to keep building the Cybertruck.
The supplier, Angstrom Automotive Group, is closing the plant and won’t let Tesla in. Tesla says that without those dies, several thousand Cybertrucks already committed to customers don’t get built.
Tesla filed the case on July 23 in the US District Court for the Western District of Texas, No. 6:26-cv-0477. The ask is narrow. Tesla isn’t going after damages and isn’t trying to settle the commercial fight underneath all this. It wants through the gate to collect its own property.
“Tesla requests the Court to grant it one thing: retrieval of Tesla’s Tooling. It does not seek to litigate any other disputes between the parties,” the company wrote in the complaint, first reported by Bloomberg Law.
The timeline in the filing is short and ugly. Angstrom’s July 13 notice that Troy was closing came with no cooperation on a plan to get Tesla’s equipment out, according to the complaint. July 17 was the ship date for 700 finished Tesla parts. They never left the building.
Then came a bill for modifications Angstrom had made to the tooling, plus an offer: the plant keeps running if $250,000 a week shows up on top of what Tesla already owes on open purchase orders.
Tesla’s answer was to send representatives to Troy on July 21 with law enforcement. The gate stayed shut.
Angstrom hasn’t commented publicly on any of it.
The equipment Tesla wants back is described in the filing as large die-cast machinery, trim dies, fixtures, cutting tools, gauges, and X-ray inspection gear. Multi-ton stuff, purpose-built for specific Cybertruck castings.
So Tesla can’t just call someone else. According to the complaint, no other supplier can currently make these parts, and rebuilding the tooling from scratch would take five to six months. Tesla also says its on-hand supply of the affected components is “dwindling and will be exhausted in mere days.”
That’s the whole leverage problem in one sentence. Whoever physically controls those dies controls the Cybertruck line, and right now that isn’t Tesla.
Angstrom is a Southfield, Michigan tier-one supplier founded in 1999, and it spent 2025 buying things. In July of last year it picked up Ontario-based KSR International, a deal Automotive News reported created a supplier with more than $1 billion in annual revenue and 4,500 employees. Then on September 9, it announced it had acquired Anderton Castings.
Anderton is the Tesla connection. The company runs aluminum die-casting operations in Troy, Texas and Monterrey, Mexico, making structural body components and EV propulsion parts like inverter housings and manifolds. Tesla’s relationship was with Anderton. Angstrom inherited it, and now Angstrom is closing the plant.
Anderton/Andstrom has not commented yet so we only have Tesla’s side of the story. I’m sure there’s more to this. It can be a complicated situation when there’s a company being taken over.
Also, we know that Tesla can be rough with suppliers and in the case of the Cybertruck, Tesla has planned production for up to 250,000 units per years and it’s only able to sell about 20,000 per year. That likely resulted in bad situations where it ordered too many parts from suppliers – resulting in screwing some people over.

title: E-quipment highlight: SANY SKT145Ei cabless, autonomous haul truck [video]
content:

It’s not just capable of driverless operation, the SANY SKT145Ei doesn’t even have a place for the driver to sit! The company’s latest all-electric heavy haul truck ditches the driver’s cab in favor of a millimeter-wave radar-guided sensor suite on a purpose-built architecture that hints at the future of zero emission mining.
Electrekkies
?) already know the mining industry has become a serious proving ground for autonomous EVs,
with hundreds of fully self-driving trucks already deployed at working mines
and many hundreds more soon to come
. The SKT145Ei takes that idea one step further, however, because instead of adapting an existing truck for autonomous operation, Chinese equipment giant SANY skipped the cab altogether, designing the vehicle around the sensors, computers, and a massive battery pack from the jump.
“Retrofitting traditional mining trucks into autonomous operation is constrained by the original architecture, making it difficult to achieve optimal placement of sensors and controllers,” explains Zhang Long from the SANY Intelligent Mining Solution team, a video posted to LinkedIn late last week. “The cabless platform is purpose-built for autonomous driving enabling more optimized layout of sensors and controllers and making inspection and maintenance easier. It has a fully driverless cabless design with reduced overall vehicle length, so it better adapts to narrow road conditions in mining areas.”
With the exception of the 801 kWh battery, SANY hasn’t published a lot of specifications. That said, the company’s current 90-ton electric mining trucks produce up to 740 kW (~990 hp) of peak power and 2,300 Nm (~1,700 lb-ft) of torque, so it’s safe to assume something similar is powering the cabless SKT145Ei.
The headline features, however, are all about safety and autonomy. “
Mining never stops for tough terrain
for darkness
, or for the challenges ahead,” adds Long. “That’s why the SKT145Ei was engineered with an 801 kWh mining-grade battery, triple-redundant braking and multi-sensor fusion perception. This model is equipped with LiDAR, mm-wave radar, and vision cameras. Multi sensor fusion technology is designed to handle harsh mining conditions such as rain, fog, and heavy dust, ensuring high vehicle availability.”

title: Taiwan introduces new solar rules for large buildings - pv magazine Global
content: Taiwan is set to bring in new rules governing the installation of solar PV systems on large buildings. From August 1, amendments to Taiwan’s Renewable Energy Development Act will require newly constructed, expanded or renovated buildings with a floor area of 1,000 square metres or more to install solar PV systems at a rate of 1 kW per 20 square metres of building area. During a briefing on the new regulations, Deputy Minister of Taiwan’s Ministry of the Interior (MOI), Dong Jian-hong, said the rules are expected to add around 660 MW of solar PV capacity annually. A news release from the MOI and Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) said the requirements will help increase the supply of green energy in urban areas while improving the energy independence and resilience of buildings with solar. The updated regulations also require solar installations to be incorporated into building plans from the design stage. This approach aims to balance aesthetics, practicality and safety, while reducing the construction and management challenges associated with adding solar systems after buildings have been completed, the ministries said. The MOI added that it will work with MOEA’s Energy Administration, Taiwan Power Company, and industry stakeholders to establish coordination mechanisms between building designers and the solar industry. The collaboration will aim to address any concerns related to equipment design, maintenance management and grid connections. “The aim is to gradually develop a comprehensive process covering solar PV planning, installation, grid connection and subsequent maintenance management, providing the industry with the necessary professional support,” the ministries said. Taiwan is on track to more than double its current solar capacity by the end of 2035, according to analysis by consultancy GlobalData, with forecasted annual growth additions between 1 GW and 2 GW. In May, the city of Taoyuan in northern Taiwan published local guidelines for solar power projects in a move signalling a shift towards a regionalized approach for solar permitting in the country. The announcement followed changes to Taiwan’s Legislative Yuan on national-level regulations governing the development of ground-mounted and floating solar projects that followed a major typhoon in July 2025, damaging over 135,000 solar panels . title: Australia adds over 700 MW of rooftop solar in April-June - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
More than 700 MW of rooftop solar was added to Australia’s main grid in the past three months, helping drive wholesale electricity prices in the country’s National Electricity Market to their lowest June quarter average since 2020.
David Carroll
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Image: Solar Victoria
Australia’s cumulative rooftop solar capacity in its National Electricity Mark (NEM) increased from 25.7 GW as of the
first quarte
r of 2026 to 26.4 GW by the end of the June quarter (Q2 2026), according to a report published by the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO). The total covers 3.9 million installations.
AEMO’s latest
Quarterly Energy Dynamics report
also shows household battery energy storage capacity across the NEM grew by almost 3.3 GWh or 41% during Q2 2026.
The report also notes 14 new grid-scale generation and storage projects totalling 3.9 GW of capacity reached full output during Q2 2026, double the previous quarterly record. This comprised 2.7 GW of battery capacity, 0.5 GW of solar-plus-battery capacity, 0.4 GW of solar capacity and 0.2 GW of wind capacity.
These supply changes lifted the renewable share of NEM generation to a new Q2 high of 42.1%, up from 37.1% in the same period last year.
Distributed PV output reached a record Q2 average of 2,520 MW, up 6.9% year-on-year, increasing its share of the energy mix to 10.3% for the quarter. Grid-scale solar generation increased by 12% to average 1,860 MW, with its share increasing to 7.6% from 6.8%, while wind output increased by 20% to 4,198 MW.
Coal generation fell 5% year-on-year to 13,158 MW, while gas-powered generation dropped 30% to its lowest Q2 average since 2003, at 1,050 MW, 30% lower than in Q2 2025.
AEMO said the record share of renewables drove average wholesale electricity prices in the NEM to their lowest June quarter average since 2020, down 47% from the same period last year to an average of AUD 74 ($51.58)/MWh.
AEMO Executive General Manager Policy and Corporate Affairs, Violette Mouchaileh, said continued investment in renewables and storage is reshaping the market. “These technologies are changing demand patterns, supporting system reliability and increasing the amount of lower-cost energy available across the market,” she said.
The same was not true for Western Australia, where the renewable share of generation declined from 33.6% to 32% for the quarter. Rooftop solar output in the Wholesale Electricity Market (WEM) increased by 3.4% but wind generation decreased by 13% due in part to lower wind speeds, while coal-fired generation fell by 17% reflecting planned and forced outages.
AEMO said these reductions increased reliance on gas-fired generation, which rose by 27%, driving average real-time wholesale electricity prices up 30% year-on-year to AUD 118/MWh.

title: As solar breaks records, its security must catch up - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
In May 2026, U.S. solar power hit a historic milestone by generating more electricity than coal for the first time, but rapid industry expansion brings critical security risks, particularly during construction, that require scalable and proactive physical defense strategies to protect valuable assets.
Jeremy White
Technology & Products
Utility-scale
Image: Pro-Vigil
, solar broke a record by doing something it had never done before in the United States: it generated more electricity than coal. According to data analyzed by energy think tank Ember, solar contributed 12.8% of the country’s electricity in May, beating out coal’s 12.2%. Additionally, solar became the third-largest source of power in the U.S., behind natural gas and nuclear.
Such a milestone provides a welcome stroke of validity to the industry. A win like this, though, measures capacity that’s already built, commissioned, and generating revenue. It doesn’t project the solar farms under construction or what the next broken record will look like. And it doesn’t say anything about whether the physical security plans for solar sites are keeping pace with how fast the industry is growing.
Solar buildout continues despite obstacles
The solar industry hasn’t experienced linear growth, and interruptions in policy can affect how the industry is set to continue growing.
According to the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA),
more than 450 solar and storage projects were bottlenecked by a slowdown in permitting.
Still, such numbers point to the industry’s sustained growth. The SEIA also projects continued growth in residential markets between 2027 and 2031.
On the ground, that means that many new construction sites across the country, starting from bare fields, will pop up for years to come. That’s the environment security planning must operate in: not after-the-fact reviews but in a forward-looking, preventative strategy, because growing industries often attract the roving eyes of thieves and vandals.
Protecting a site during construction
Often, the greatest exposure for a solar farm is during construction, before permanent power, fencing, and staff are in place. During this phase, equipment, panels, and copper wiring are sitting on an open site with little to slow a bad actor down.
The fence perimeter that will eventually circumvent a finished site (if implemented at all) is often not yet erected, or if it is, it only exists in sections, leaving the most theft-prone materials open to the elements and to the thieves hungry for a quick profit.
In May of this year
, a man was charged with stealing 2,000 feet of copper wiring and dozens of connectors from two solar farms in North Carolina after cutting through perimeter fencing. Losses on two different sites amounted to $11,000.
Traditional security measures for sites, such as fencing, lightning, and warning signage, all still matter, but their fail point is twofold: they’re designed for finished sites and they lack an additional preventative measure.
For remote solar sites
under construction, a comprehensive security strategy must exist before the panels and copper arrive. It can’t wait until the day the site goes live.
Rightsizing physical security
Scale presents a particular problem. Security plans designed for 10-acre solar farms don’t apply at 500 acres. They break. A handful of cameras and a light monitoring routine might be enough to adequately cover a 10-acre site, but if you multiply that footprint by fifty, the math doesn’t scale in a straight line. Camera count, monitoring load, and response protocols all have to be redesigned, not simply expanded.
Ten times the perimeter doesn’t mean you need ten times the cameras. It means you need a monitoring approach that can still distinguish a legitimate, after-hours technician from an intruder on a site of that size. And you still need to be able to respond in seconds rather than minutes or more.
Proactive security that grows with the site
Often, many businesses won’t invest in a proactive security strategy until an incident resulting in monetary loss forces their hand. A truly proactive security strategy is
a layered one
. In practice, that means combining multiple tools, technologies, and obstacles to create a robust system that not only catches thieves in action but
them and prevents crime.
This can start with perimeter fences and incorporates cameras. In today’s security, monitored units are preferable to simple record-and-store cameras. Video surveillance tools can either be
(for sites with ready access to internet, places with brick-and-mortar buildings) or
(which are better for remote areas that lack access to Wi-Fi).
For solar farms, mobile surveillance units tend to work better as they provide connected access for remote areas and can be moved to support a continuously evolving strategy. Because they don’t require permanent power or wiring, mobile surveillance units can accompany a solar site at any stage: from the early days of construction through to daily operation once construction is complete and the site is in full swing.
As the project’s surface area expands during construction, additional mobile units can be deployed to keep eyes on the riskiest entry points simultaneously.
But it’s what occurs on the other side of those camera lenses that turns a reactive security strategy into a proactive one. Mobile surveillance units are equipped with
AI-powered detection
which is trained to distinguish between an access-permitted contractor and a would-be thief cutting through the fence line.
When detection is escalated for a threat, a trained human monitor confirms that a threat is in fact on the premises, and they can cue
audio and visual deterrents
to ward off the thief.
As a site grows, having this layered strategy ensures a methodical and pragmatic approach to a solar farm’s physical security, helping to deter thieves
they intend to act. And when a site is complete and fully operational, a layered security strategy helps to prevent damage, theft, and loss.
Solar overtaking coal in May was a big moment, and it’s a clue into the growth the industry is set to experience. As the industry continues to expand, the target on its back grows as well. With projects set to take place, the time to invest in a proactive security strategy is before the project breaks ground, not after an incident occurs.
